title: Protected Areas, Biodiversity Hotspots and Endangered Species
topicTitle: National parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, biodiversity hotspots, wetland and Ramsar sites; wildlife: importance, causes of extinction and conservation strategies; IUCN categories of threatened species: meaning of extinct, endangered, vulnerable, rare and threatened species; endangered species in Nepal
notes: **Protected area categories:** national park (strict protection, no resource extraction), wildlife reserve (limited traditional use allowed), conservation area (multiple use, community participation).
**Ramsar sites:** wetlands of international importance designated under Ramsar Convention. Nepal has 9 Ramsar sites including Ghodaghodi Tal, Gokyo lakes, Koshi Tappu.
**IUCN Red List categories:** Extinct (EX), Extinct in Wild (EW), Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), Vulnerable (VU), Near Threatened (NT), Least Concern (LC).
**Causes of extinction:** habitat loss (deforestation, wetland drainage), overexploitation (poaching, overfishing), pollution, invasive species, climate change.
**Conservation strategies:** habitat protection, captive breeding and reintroduction, legislation (CITES, Wildlife Act), community-based conservation, ecotourism, education.

**Endangered species in Nepal:** Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris), one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis), snow leopard (Panthera uncia), red panda (Ailurus fulgens), Himalayan musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster).

**Nepal's protected area network:** Covers approximately 21% of Nepal's total land area. Includes 10 national parks, 4 wildlife reserves, 3 conservation areas, and 1 hunting reserve. Chitwan National Park (1973) and Sagarmatha National Park (1976) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

**Wetland ecosystem services:** Wetlands filter pollutants, recharge groundwater, control flooding, sequester carbon (peatlands store twice as much carbon as all forests combined), and support fisheries and agriculture. They are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.

**IUCN criteria for threatened categories:** CR: >80% population decline over 10 years/3 generations; EN: >50% decline; VU: >30% decline. Population size thresholds also apply (e.g., EN: <2500 mature individuals). These quantitative criteria help standardize assessments globally.

**CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species):** An international agreement regulating trade in wild animals and plants. Nepal's tiger and rhino trade is listed under CITES Appendix I, the strictest category, banning commercial international trade.

**Community forestry in Nepal:** A globally recognized model where local communities manage forest resources. Over 22,000 community forest user groups manage about 2.3 million hectares, contributing significantly to forest cover recovery and biodiversity conservation.

**Ecotourism and conservation:** Wildlife tourism generates revenue that funds protected area management and provides alternative livelihoods. In Nepal, tiger and rhino tourism in Chitwan and Bardia has helped reverse population declines from poaching.

**Rare vs. threatened species:** Rare species have small population sizes or limited distributions but are not necessarily declining. Threatened species (CR, EN, VU) meet quantitative criteria for vulnerability to extinction. All threatened species are at risk, but not all rare species are immediately threatened.

**Invasive species in Nepal:** Lantana camara, Parthenium hysterophorus, and water hyacinth are invasive plants that threaten native biodiversity by outcompeting endemic species and altering habitats. Invasive species are the second leading cause of extinction globally.
confusion: A national park is not the same as a wildlife reserve — national parks prohibit resource extraction and human settlement, while wildlife reserves may allow sustainable traditional use by local communities.

Ramsar sites are not just any wetland — they must meet specific international criteria for ecological, botanical, or zoological importance. Only about 2,500 of the world's wetlands are Ramsar-designated.

Extinct (EX) means the last individual has died; Extinct in the Wild (EW) means the species survives only in captivity or cultivation. The scimitar-horned oryx is EW — wild populations died out but captive breeds exist.

Climate change is a cause of extinction but operates differently from habitat loss — it alters the conditions species are adapted to, rather than destroying their habitat directly. Range shifts and phenology mismatches are key mechanisms.

Nepal's one-horned rhinoceros is Endangered (EN) globally but was Vulnerable (VU) in Nepal's 2017 assessment — conservation efforts in Chitwan and Bardia have significantly improved its status, showing that targeted action can reverse decline.
practice: Match each IUCN category to its correct definition: (a) Extinct, (b) Critically Endangered, (c) Vulnerable, (d) Least Concern. Then explain why a species might move from VU to EN between assessments.
A wetland near a city is being drained for agriculture. List three ecosystem services that would be lost and explain how each loss would affect local people.
Nepal has 9 Ramsar sites. Choose one and describe: (a) its location, (b) why it was designated, (c) threats it faces, (d) one conservation action needed.
Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation for the snow leopard. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each approach for this species?
A community forestry group wants to allow limited timber harvesting. Using the principles of sustainable use, outline the conditions under which this would be acceptable.
universalFacts: Nepal's one-horned rhinoceros population grew from approximately 100 in the 1960s to over 750 in 2023 — one of the most successful conservation recoveries in South Asia.
The Nepal Tiger Initiative aims to double the wild tiger population by 2022 (the year of the tiger); the 2022 census recorded 330 tigers, up from 121 in 2009.
Bardia National Park, Nepal's largest lowland national park, is home to the highest density of tigers in the country and serves as a critical source population for the entire Terai landscape.
The Himalaya biodiversity hotspot encompasses 12 countries and holds over 10,000 vascular plant species, 600 bird species, and 170 mammal species, with high rates of endemism.

Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, Nepal's only Ramsar site in the eastern Terai, supports over 500 bird species including the vulnerable Bengal florican and is critical for migratory waterfowl along the Central Asian flyway.
